content: Hemorrhagic disease of the newborn, also known as vitamin K deficiency bleeding, is a coagulation disorder that occurs in newborns due to a deficiency of vitamin K. This deficiency leads to impaired production of several coagulation factors, specifically factors II, VII, IX, X, as well as proteins C and S, which are synthesized in the liver. Newborns are particularly prone to vitamin K deficiency for several reasons. At birth, their vitamin K stores are naturally low. Additionally, vitamin K does not cross the placenta efficiently during pregnancy. Breast milk contains only minimal amounts of vitamin K, and the intestinal flora, which normally produces vitamin K, has not yet developed in newborns. The primary clinical manifestation of this condition is an increased risk of bleeding. Common sites of bleeding include the umbilical stump, mucous membranes, the gastrointestinal tract, circumcision sites, and areas of venipuncture. The treatment for hemorrhagic disease of the newborn involves supplementation with vitamin K. In many cases, vitamin K is administered prophylactically to newborns shortly after birth to prevent the development of this condition.
